title: A flatmate's sore throat
stem:
You are an F2 doctor. Your flatmate has had a sore throat for three days. She says she can't get a GP appointment this week.

She asks you to write her a prescription for antibiotics, saying, "You're a doctor, so it'll be quicker."
instruction: Choose the 3 most appropriate actions to take in this situation.

options.text: Explain kindly that you can't prescribe for her.
options.brief: Prescribing for friends should be avoided.
options.detailed: You aren't her doctor, you haven't assessed her properly, and you don't have her records. Prescribing for friends risks poor care and blurs boundaries.

options.text: Write the prescription, as sore throats are usually minor.
options.brief: Prescribing for a friend without assessment isn't appropriate.
options.detailed: Even for minor conditions, prescribing for friends risks poor care, and most sore throats don't need antibiotics.

options.text: Give her some antibiotics left over from your own course.
options.detailed: Leftover antibiotics may be the wrong drug, dose or duration, and sharing prescribed medicines is unsafe.

options.text: Examine her throat and prescribe if it looks infected.
options.brief: You'd be taking on her care informally.
options.detailed: This makes you her doctor without proper records, consent or follow-up, which is what the guidance warns against.

options.text: Ask a colleague at work to prescribe for her.
options.brief: Still prescribing outside a proper consultation.
options.detailed: Your colleague wouldn't be her doctor either, and this just passes the problem on.

options.text: Suggest she sees a pharmacist about her sore throat.
options.brief: Pharmacists can assess sore throats and supply treatment if needed.
options.detailed: Many pharmacies can assess sore throats and, in some cases, supply antibiotics. This is a quick, appropriate route.

options.text: Tell her when she should seek urgent help.
options.brief: Useful safety advice that doesn't make you her doctor.
options.detailed: General advice on when to seek urgent help is a reasonable thing for a friend to share and keeps her safe.

options.text: Tell her antibiotics never help sore throats.
options.detailed: Most sore throats don't need antibiotics, but some do. Overstating it may stop her seeking help when she needs it.

explanation.issue: This tests whether you keep appropriate boundaries when a friend asks you to prescribe, while still helping her get care.
explanation.keyDetails: She is a friend, not your patient. It isn't an emergency. Other routes to care exist.
explanation.reasoning: [A] declines kindly, [F] points her to an appropriate route, and [G] gives safety advice. The distractors prescribe inappropriately ([B], [C], [D], [E]) or give inaccurate information ([H]).
explanation.competing: [D] feels like a careful compromise, but it still makes you her doctor informally.

references.title: Good practice in proposing, prescribing, providing and managing medicines and devices
references.note: Avoiding prescribing for yourself or those close to you.
